cell: Start with a single leaf. The widest part is the blade. A stalk, the petiole, holds it to the stem. See the line down the middle? That is the midrib, and it branches out to each side into veins. Those veins are the leaf's supply lines. Water and minerals come in, and the products of photosynthesis go out, to the rest of the tree.

Now we cut into the blade. A skin of cells, the epidermis, covers both sides of the leaf, and it is usually just one layer of cells. Under the upper side, palisade cells stand like columns, packed tightly together. Below them, the spongy cells are arranged loosely, and leave air spaces. Both layers hold many chloroplasts. And on the underside: stomata, pores in the lower epidermis that let gases pass. Each one has two guard cells, which open it and close it.

Here is one palisade cell, taken apart piece by piece. On the outside, the cell wall. It protects the cell and gives it its shape. Then the plasma membrane, which controls what passes in and out. The chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis. The central vacuole takes up most of the cell's volume, and regulates its water. The nucleus holds the cell's DNA. And the mitochondria make ATP, the cell's main energy carrier. Three of these parts, an animal cell does not have: the cell wall, the chloroplasts, and the central vacuole.

Closer still: a single chloroplast. Inside its double envelope lie stacks of disc-shaped thylakoids. Now watch what flows. Light, carbon dioxide and water go in. Sugar and oxygen come out. And here is the surprising part. Carbon taken from the air makes up most of a tree's dry mass.
section: Let's open a window in the trunk. On the outside, the bark. It shields the tree from heat, cold, rain and insects. Then the phloem, which carries food from the leaves to the rest of the tree. Just inside the phloem lies the cambium. It makes new wood, and new bark. Further in, the sapwood carries water up from the roots. And in the centre, the heartwood. It is dead, and it holds the tree up. Now look at the rings. Each pair, one light and one dark, is one year of growth.

So where is the tree alive? Here, the glowing cells are alive, and the pale ones are dead. The phloem cells are alive. The cambium cells are alive too, and they keep dividing. In the sapwood, it is mixed: the cells that carry the water are dead, but the parenchyma cells are alive. And in the heartwood, every cell is dead.

This is how a trunk grows. The cambium cells divide. On the inside they form new wood, and on the outside, new phloem. So the trunk grows wider. The new water-carrying cells die as they mature. And over time, the phloem becomes part of the bark.

Now follow the water on its way up. These water-carrying cells are tracheids. Their thick walls contain lignin, a key part of wood. Watch the drops. They move from one tracheid to the next, through pits in the side walls. And what moves them? Water evaporates from the leaves, and that pulls the water up from the roots.

Sugar travels the other way. In the phloem, sieve-tube cells sit end to end, and form one long sieve tube. Between them are sieve plates, and the sugars flow through their holes, from one cell to the next. Pressure pushes the sugar and water down, toward the roots. These sieve-tube cells are alive, but they have lost their nucleus. So they get help: the companion cells next to them give them energy.

Closer now, into a single pit. A pit is a place in the side wall where the thick secondary wall is missing. And at this scale, the water is no longer drops. It is molecules. They hold on to each other, and they hold on to the cell walls. So the water forms one continuous stream, from the base of the tree, all the way to the top.
rock: Down here, at the very tip of a root. A root cap protects the tip as it pushes through the soil. Behind it grow the root hairs. They grow from the outer cells, and they increase the root's surface area for taking up water and minerals. But there is a problem. The soil right around the roots can run low in nutrients. So most plants rely on a partner: fungi.

Meet the partner. Most plants live with fungal partners on their roots. They are called mycorrhizae. On pines and other forest trees, the fungus wraps the root tip in a sheath, the mantle. From there, thread-like hyphae spread far beyond the root hairs. They are much finer than roots. And some of them grow onto grains of rock.

Can a fungus dissolve rock? In one lab study, Scots pine seedlings grew with a fungus, and only its threads could reach the grains of rock. The threads released oxalate, an organic acid. And calcium dissolved out of the grains. Much of it formed crystals of calcium oxalate, right on the threads. How much depended on the rock: least on quartz and granite, most on gabbro. What you see here is sped up. The experiment ran for three to four months.

So what does each side get? It is a trade. Sugars made in the leaves travel down through the root, to the fungus. In return, the threads bring the tree minerals, such as phosphorus. And in the pine study, the fungus did not share that sugar evenly. It sent more of the tree's sugar to grains rich in calcium and magnesium than to quartz.

Back to the root itself, and to one root hair. A root hair is not a separate thing. It is an extension of a single cell of the root's outer layer, the epidermis. Water moves from the soil into the root's cells by osmosis. And all these hairs enlarge the root's surface, which greatly helps it absorb water and minerals.

Now we cut the root open. Follow the water inward. It crosses the cortex, and then it reaches a ring of cells: the endodermis. Here, it cannot slip between the cells. A waxy band in their walls, the Casparian strip, stops it. The water has to pass through the cells themselves. So the endodermis is a checkpoint for what enters the root's vascular tissue. And inside the ring, the xylem carries the water up, into the tree.
water: Here is a puzzle. Coast redwoods grow to nearly one hundred and sixteen metres, and water still reaches their highest leaves. Gravity pulls on that water the whole way up. And yet, lifting it costs the tree no metabolic energy. So how does it get there? The pull starts at the top.

It starts in the leaf. Inside, water evaporates from wet cell walls, into the air spaces. The vapour escapes through pores called stomata. This loss has a name: transpiration. And the evaporation creates a tension that pulls on the water in the xylem.

What holds the water together? Water molecules hold on to each other. That is cohesion. And they hold on to the walls of the xylem. That is adhesion. So the water forms one continuous stream, from the base to the top, and the pull lifts all of it. This is the cohesion-tension theory.

And at the bottom, new water comes in. Root cells hold many dissolved substances, so water moves into them from the soil, by osmosis. It enters through the root hairs, and it replaces the water lost from the leaves. And a lot is lost. Up to ninety percent of the water the roots take up may be lost through transpiration.

Water is not the only thing on the move. Leaves make sugars, such as sucrose, by photosynthesis. The phloem carries them to where they are used or stored. That is called translocation. Lower leaves send their sugar down, to the roots. Water in the xylem is different. It only moves one way: from soil, to leaf, to air.
